lines: Tap a painting, then tap a seat, then tap Take your seat.
We start by describing. Tap Pin on a claim, then tap the spot in the painting that shows it.
If a claim can't be pinned, tap Challenge and pick the reason.
Now build your own claim with the menus, then tap Pin it.
The floor is clear. Tap Next round.
Now analyze how the parts work together. Pin each claim to its spot, or challenge it.
Now interpret what it might mean. Pin each claim to the spot that shows why, or challenge it.
Now judge. Pick a lens first, then pin each claim or challenge it.
On the record.
That spot doesn't show it. Tap another spot, or tap Cancel and challenge it.
That pin does not support your sentence. Tap another spot, or tap Cancel to revise your menus.
This belongs to a later round. Tap Challenge and pick Wrong round.
Not under this lens. Switch the lens, then pin it.
Struck from the record.
Look again at what kind of claim this is.
The record is ready. Edit your piece, then tap Print or New panel.
Tap Pin on a claim, or Challenge it. Build one claim of your own.
Pick a painting and a seat first.
Tap the reason this claim cannot go on the record.
Tap Pin on this claim, or tap Challenge.
Claim reopened. Tap Pin or Challenge.
Your claim was removed. Build another claim, then tap Pin it.
Build another sentence with the menus, then tap Pin it.
Pick a lens above the floor first. Then tap Pin.
Two spots selected. Tap a selected spot to remove it, or tap Done.
Pin cancelled. Tap Pin or Challenge, or build your own claim.
On the record. Pin or challenge the remaining claims; add one of your own.
Struck from the record. Read the reply, then pin or challenge another claim.
Challenge closed. Tap Pin or Challenge on this claim.
Two people share one umbrella and walk toward us on the right.
A green lamppost stands right in the middle of the picture.
This is a lonely, sad painting.
Fair. I'll save that for interpreting.
The lamppost and its shadow cut the picture into two halves.
The lines of the buildings run far back, so the square feels huge.
The man at the right edge is cut off, like a quick photo.
The city is crowded, but no one talks to anyone.
Caillebotte hated the new Paris.
You're right, the picture alone can't tell us what he felt.
The wet stones and gray light make it feel quiet and cool.
It works because every part is placed so carefully.
This is the greatest painting of the 1800s.
Too big a claim. I'll narrow it.
It feels real enough to step into.
A man lies on the deck of a small boat with a broken mast.
Sharks circle the boat.
Homer is warning us about the sea.
That's an interpretation. I'll hold it.
The boat tilts on a diagonal, so nothing feels steady.
The waterspout and the far ship sit on opposite sides, pulling the eye across.
The man lies at the center, with every danger placed around him.
The far ship could be rescue, or it could be passing by. Homer leaves it open.
The man is calm while danger closes in from every side.
The sugar cane tells us this was a working boat.
It is powerful because it makes me fear for him.
The painting was ruined when Homer reworked it.
I can't show that in the picture. The label only says he reworked it.
It's the best sea painting ever made.
I'll argue the case, not the trophy.
A woman washes a child's feet in a basin.
Both of them look down at the water.
This is about how much she loves the child.
Agreed, that's for later.
We look down from above, so the floor tilts up and fills the picture.
Stripes, rug and wallpaper make patterns everywhere.
Their two heads and the basin form a tight triangle.
Their shared downward look makes a small, quiet moment feel important.
Cassatt copied this pose from a Japanese print.
Influence, maybe, but I can't prove copying from the picture.
The pitcher and basin make it an everyday task, not a special event.
It's well designed: the patterns and the tilted floor hold together.
It does a job: it shows care as real work worth painting.
Women's art is always gentler.
That's a generalization, not a reading of this painting. Withdrawn.
